t.2.1: Saṃjaya said: To him, thus overcome with pity, his eyes troubled and filled with tears, and sinking in despair, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
t.2.2: The Blessed Lord said: Whence has this weakness come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is not practiced by the noble, it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
t.2.3: Do not yield to unmanliness, Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, scorcher of foes!
t.2.4: Arjuna said: O Madhusūdana, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are both worthy of worship, O slayer of enemies?
t.2.5: Better indeed to eat even alms-food here in this world than to slay these noble-souled teachers; for having slain my teachers, though they are bent on gain, I would here enjoy only pleasures smeared with blood.
t.2.7: My very nature stricken by the fault of faint-hearted pity, my mind utterly confused about dharma, I ask you: tell me decisively what would be better. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
t.2.6: Nor do we know which is better for us, whether we should conquer them or whether they should conquer us. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand before us, the very ones after slaying whom we would not wish to live.
t.2.8: For I do not see what could drive away this grief of mine that dries up my senses, even if I were to obtain on earth an unrivaled, prosperous kingdom, and even sovereignty over the gods.
t.2.9: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, O scorcher of foes, Guḍākeśa said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and fell silent.
t.2.10: O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of both armies.
t.2.11: The Blessed Lord said: You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for those whose life has departed nor for those whose life has not departed.
t.2.12: Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
t.2.13: Just as, for the embodied one, there are childhood, youth and old age in this body, so too there is the attainment of another body; the steadfast one is not deluded by this.
t.2.14: But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O Kaunteya, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go and are impermanent. Endure them, O Bhārata.
t.2.15: O bull among men, the steadfast person whom these do not disturb, who remains the same in sorrow and in joy, is fit for immortality.
t.2.16: Of the unreal there is no being, and of the real there is no non-being; the final truth of both of these has been seen by the seers of reality.
t.2.17: But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable one.
t.2.18: These bodies of the eternal embodied one, who is imperishable and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Bhārata.
t.2.19: He who thinks this one to be a slayer, and he who thinks this one to be slain, both of them do not understand: this one neither slays nor is slain.
t.2.20: He is never born, nor does he ever die; nor, having come to be, will he ever cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and primeval, he is not slain when the body is slain.
t.2.21: He who knows this to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and imperishable, how, O Pārtha, can that person cause anyone to be slain, or slay anyone?
t.2.22: Just as a man casts off worn-out garments and takes on other, new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and enters into others that are new.
t.2.23: Weapons do not cut this one, fire does not burn this one, waters do not wet this one, and wind does not dry it up.
t.2.24: This Self cannot be cut, this cannot be burned, cannot be wetted, and cannot be dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and everlasting.
t.2.25: This is said to be unmanifest, this is unthinkable, this is unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve.
t.2.26: And even if you think of this self as constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for it.
t.2.27: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. Therefore, over a matter that cannot be avoided, you ought not to grieve.
t.2.28: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle, and unmanifest again in their end, O Bhārata; what lamentation can there be over this?
t.2.29: One sees him as a wonder, another likewise speaks of him as a wonder, and another hears of him as a wonder; yet even having heard of him, no one knows him at all.
t.2.30: This embodied one dwelling in the body of everyone is eternally unslayable, O Bhārata; therefore you ought not to grieve for any creatures.
t.2.31: And considering your own duty as well, you ought not to waver, for there exists nothing better for a kṣatriya than a righteous war.
t.2.33: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own duty and your honor, you will incur sin.
t.2.34: Moreover, all beings will speak of your undying disgrace, and for one who has been held in honor, disgrace is worse than death.
t.2.32: Happy are the kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a battle, come of its own accord, an open door to heaven.
t.2.35: The great chariot-warriors will think that you withdrew from battle out of fear, and you, having been highly esteemed by them, will fall into lightness.
t.2.36: Your enemies will speak many words that ought not to be spoken, disparaging your ability. What, indeed, could be more painful than that?
t.2.37: Slain, you will attain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O Kaunteya, resolved upon battle.
t.2.38: Treating alike pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, then gird yourself for battle; thus you will not incur sin.
t.2.39: This understanding has been declared to you in terms of Sāṃkhya; now hear it in terms of Yoga, O Pārtha, for joined with this understanding you will cast off the bondage of action.
t.2.40: Here no effort that is begun is ever lost, and no adverse result is found. Even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
t.2.41: Here, O Kurunandana, the resolute understanding is one, but many-branched and endless are the understandings of the irresolute.
t.2.42: O Pārtha, the unwise, who delight in the words of the Veda and declare that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech.
t.2.44: For those who cling to pleasure and power, whose minds are carried away by that flowery speech, the resolute understanding is not established in samādhi.
t.2.43: Their minds full of desire and heaven their highest goal, they proclaim a speech that offers rebirth as the fruit of action, abounds in elaborate rites, and aims at the attainment of pleasure and power.
t.2.45: The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna, free from the pairs of opposites, ever established in sattva, free from concern for acquiring and keeping, and possessed of the Self.
t.2.46: As much use as there is in a small well when there is water flooding on every side, so much use is there in all the Vedas for a brāhmaṇa who truly knows.
t.2.47: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruits of action be your motive, and let there be no attachment in you to inaction.
t.2.48: Established in yoga, perform your actions, Dhanaṃjaya, having abandoned attachment and having become even-minded in success and failure; evenness of mind is called yoga.
t.2.49: Far inferior indeed is action to the yoga of understanding, O Dhanaṃjaya; seek refuge in understanding. Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
t.2.50: One who is yoked to understanding casts off, here in this world, both good deeds and evil deeds. Therefore, yoke yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions.
t.2.51: For the wise, yoked to understanding, having abandoned the fruit born of action and freed from the bondage of birth, go to the state beyond all sorrow.
t.2.52: When your intellect crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
t.2.53: When your understanding, now bewildered by what you have heard of scripture, stands firm and unwavering, immovable in samādhi, then you will attain yoga.
t.2.54: Arjuna said: O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi? How does one of steady mind speak, how does he sit, and how does he walk?
t.2.55: The Blessed Lord said: When one wholly casts off all the desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha, and is content in the Self by the Self alone, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
t.2.56: One whose mind is not shaken amid sorrows, who is free from craving amid pleasures, and from whom passion, fear and anger have departed, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
t.2.57: He who is without attachment everywhere, who, on meeting with this or that, good or evil, neither rejoices nor hates, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.58: When he withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, then his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.59: The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from them, but the taste for them remains; yet even that taste of his turns away once he has seen the Supreme.
t.2.60: For even of a discerning man who strives, O Kaunteya, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind.
t.2.61: Having restrained them all, he should sit disciplined, intent on me; for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.62: For a man who dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger springs forth.
t.2.63: From anger arises delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from the loss of memory, the destruction of intelligence; and with the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.
t.2.64: But the self-controlled one, moving among the objects of sense with senses freed from attachment and aversion and governed by the self, attains serenity.
t.2.65: In serenity, the destruction of all his sorrows comes about; for the understanding of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established.
t.2.66: For one who is not disciplined there is no understanding, and for the undisciplined there is no contemplation; for one who does not contemplate there is no peace, and for one without peace, whence can happiness come?
t.2.67: For when the mind is made to follow the roving senses, it carries away his wisdom, as the wind carries away a ship on the waters.
t.2.68: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.69: What is night for all beings, in that the self-controlled one is awake; that in which beings are awake is night for the seeing sage.
t.2.70: As the waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet remains unmoved in its foundation, so the one whom all desires enter in the same way attains peace, not the one who longs after desires.
t.2.71: The man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.
t.2.72: This, O Pārtha, is the state of Brahman; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Abiding in it even at the time of death, one reaches the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
